summary: Discovery call to scope a POC benchmarking plan. Focus was aligning on which latency metrics matter (TTFT vs TPOT), realistic p95/p99 targets for Atlas Retail's bursty traffic, and how we'll measure them end-to-end. Agreed next steps: exchange traces, Redwood provides harness + measurement scripts, schedule baseline run the week of Sep 8.
transcript:
Date: 2025-08-27 15:30 UTC | Duration: 54m | Recorded on Fireflies
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Sharma (Atlas Retail - Head of ML), Liam O'Connor (Infra Lead), Rosa Martinez (Product), Kevin (intern)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick roll call — Maya from Redwood here, Daniel our SE is on. Priya, Liam, Rosa, you there?
[00:12] Priya: Yep, hi all. Thanks, Maya. We wanted to tighten up SLOs for our checkout recommender, mostly concerned about tail latency during promo spikes.
[00:21] Daniel: Got it. We'll talk TTFT and TPOT definitions, figure out the traffic shape, and propose an EMR-like — sorry, a measurement plan.
[00:30] Liam: Small correction, we use KEDA for autoscale not EMR. But yeah, spikes are the issue.
[00:36] Rosa: Also product is worried about UX — p99 spikes cause timeouts in the mobile app.
[00:42] Maya: Understood. Quick framing: TTFT is time-to-first-token — useful for interactive flows. TPOT is time-per-output-token or throughput-focused metric. For your recommender, we usually care about both: TTFT for cold requests and TPOT for sustained throughput.
[01:05] Priya: Can you give an example tradeoff? Like if we optimize TTFT, do we lose throughput?
[01:12] Daniel: Yeah, sometimes. For strict TTFT you might pin models on low-batch, low-latency runners which reduces batching efficiency. For TPOT you allow more batching or async queues, improving tokens/sec but increasing first-token latency. There's also caching/prefix KV strategies that help both.
[01:35] Liam: Our traffic is very bursty: 20k qps for 30s during flash sales, then quiet. So average numbers obscure tail behavior.
[01:43] Maya: That matters. For bursty workloads we often set two SLOs: a cold TTFT p95/p99 target and a warm TPOT p95 target during sustained bursts.
[01:55] Priya: What's realistic? We currently see p95 ~420ms and p99 ~1.2s on our prototype infra. We want p99 under 800ms ideally. Is that feasible?
[02:08] Daniel: Depends on model and infra. For a 7B decoder-only model quantized to int8 on A100-ish hardware, 800ms p99 for TTFT might be tight during cold spikes unless you provision dedicated capacity. If you use warm pools + KV cache, we can often hit ~500ms p95 and ~800-900ms p99.
[02:30] Rosa: Dedicated sounds expensive. Can we do hybrid?
[02:34] Maya: Yes — Redwood Dedicated with burst capacity is exactly that: baseline shared, reserved pools for steady state, and short-term burst to meet p99 during known events. We'll model cost vs provisioning.
[02:44] Liam: On measurement: do you replay traces or synthetic load?
[02:49] Daniel: We recommend a 3-pronged approach: 1) replay real production traces (sanitized) to capture distribution; 2) controlled synthetic bursts to stress tails; 3) microbench kernels to validate model runtime characteristics.
[03:02] Priya: We'll prefer replay; we can provide a 1-hour trace from last sale. Any special format?
[03:07] Daniel: Common format is JSON lines with timestamp, request_id, prompt_template_id, and token length. We can accept gzipped traces. We'll give a template.
[03:15] Maya: For success criteria — let's be explicit: acceptance if baseline run demonstrates TTFT p99 <= 800ms for 95% of burst windows and TPOT during sustained 30s windows >= X tokens/sec (we'll propose X after we see token lengths). Also quality regressions < 2% on your eval prompts.
[03:34] Rosa: Quality regression — is that a semantic similarity check? We run human evals too.
[03:38] Daniel: We typically use a combination of automated embeddings-based similarity plus human spot checks on a sample of prompts. We'll align on the eval harness.
[03:46] Priya: Ok. Timeline — when can we run the baseline?
[03:49] Maya: If we get traces and prompts by Sep 4, Redwood can prepare harness and run baseline the week of Sep 8; results + cost estimates by Sep 12.
[03:57] Liam: Security — we need to know about key management and audit logs for the POC.
[04:01] Maya: We'll attach SOC2 snapshot and describe KMS integration. For the POC we'll accept encrypted payload at rest and TLS in transit; logs scrubbed for PII.
[04:10] Priya: Great. Quick deep-dive on metric extraction: how do you calculate p99 across a burst window?
[04:16] Daniel: We slide fixed-length windows across the run — e.g., 30s windows — and compute per-window p95/p99 for TTFT and aggregate across windows. For TPOT we measure tokens/sec per worker and compute p95 of throughput distribution. We also report cold vs warm breakdown via cache-hit labels.
[04:36] Rosa: How do you label cold vs warm?
[04:39] Daniel: We inject synthetic warmup requests and keep a KV cache TTL; warm = KV hit in under 10ms. We also mark requests that hit a warmed worker vs ones that required model load.
[04:52] Priya: Any gotchas with measuring on-prem vs hosted? We have a hybrid infra partially on GCP.
[04:59] Maya: For hybrid, we recommend measuring end-to-end from your client to Redwood endpoints to capture networking hops. If you run Redwood Private on VPC, we can run the harness inside your network to emulate true latencies.
[05:12] Liam: We might need to VPC peer for the pilot. I'll follow up with peering details.
[05:17] Kevin: (quiet) should we anonymize user IDs?
[05:19] Priya: Yes, we'll scrub PII before sharing.
[05:22] Maya: Back to SLO numbers — let's sketch a conservative, stretch, and cost-optimized target: conservative TTFT p95 600ms / p99 1.0s; stretch p95 400ms / p99 700ms; cost-optimized p95 800ms / p99 1.6s but with lower reserved capacity. Thoughts?
[05:44] Priya: That helps. Stretch looks ideal but maybe costly. We'll likely aim for conservative as minimum.
[05:50] Daniel: We'll also capture TPOT targets: tokens/sec per replica during 30s burst windows. Need your average token-per-request number.
[05:59] Priya: Average tokens per request in recommender is low — 18 tokens on avg, but worst-case up to 120 for long contextual prompts.
[06:08] Daniel: Ok we'll calibrate. For small token sizes TPOT isn't as critical as TTFT, but for long-context requests throughput matters more. 
[06:18] Rosa: For the baseline, can you run two model variants? One quantized 4-bit, one int8? We want to compare cost/latency/quality.
[06:26] Maya: Yes. Redwood can run both variants and provide delta analysis. We'll note any quality deltas.
[06:32] Priya: How do we handle reroutes if you can't meet p99 during live events?
[06:36] Maya: Redwood supports automatic fallback policies: degrade to smaller model, route to a cached response, or spike to reserved burst pool. We'll propose a fallback plan for your SLOs.
[06:45] Liam: What about instrumentation — do you need us to add headers or trace IDs?
[06:49] Daniel: Yes, include a tracing header for request_id and a cache-hit header in responses. We'll provide an instrumentation snippet.
[06:58] Priya: Are the measurement scripts open-source?
[07:01] Maya: We'll share a lightweight harness (open-source MIT) and a Redwood-owned benchmark runner config. The harness is config-driven so you can replay traces locally too.
[07:10] Priya: Good. On the subject of windows — you mentioned 30s windows. Could we also look at 5s windows for super-short spikes?
[07:16] Daniel: Absolutely. We'll produce metrics for multiple window granularities: 5s, 30s, 5m. That's important for your flash sales.
[07:26] Rosa: What's the recommended sample size for human evals to detect a 2% regression with reasonable confidence?
[07:31] Daniel: Roughly 400 judgments per variant for ~95% power to detect a 2-3% delta, assuming independent samples. We can help design the A/B eval.
[07:43] Priya: Budget note — if we need dedicated capacity for a day during a sale, what does burst pricing look like?
[07:49] Maya: We'll provide a cost model after baseline. Rough ballpark: short-term burst instances billed at higher per-minute rate; we'll give cost-per-1k-requests estimate based on run.
[07:58] Liam: Ok. Any legal constraints? We have data residency requirements in EU for certain segments.
[08:03] Maya: For EU data residency we can run Redwood Private in a EU region or on-prem. For the POC, if the trace contains EU PII we'll mask or run the harness within your EU VPC.
[08:13] Priya: Good. Quick check: we want the final artifact to include a measurement plan doc, raw run CSVs, cost model, and suggested rollout plan.
[08:20] Maya: We'll deliver that.
[08:22] (silence ~5s)
[08:27] Kevin: tiny question — are network cold-starts a big part of TTFT?
[08:30] Daniel: They can be, especially with cross-region peering; that's why we recommend end-to-end measurement including client round-trip.
[08:37] Priya: Let's talk about what constitutes a 'failure' during the POC. We need a clear stop/go criteria.
[08:42] Maya: Proposal: Stop condition if baseline run shows p99 > 2x the agreed conservative target (i.e., >2s) or if quality regression >5% on evaluated prompts; otherwise proceed and iterate.
[08:55] Rosa: Seems fair.
[08:57] Priya: Any recommended synthetic spike shapes? We have historical shape data but not sure how to translate to load profiles.
[09:03] Daniel: We use a mix: delta spike (instant ramp), ramp-up (over 15s), and sustained plateau (30s). We'll map your trace percentiles to these shapes.
[09:13] Maya: Ok quickly recapping next steps so we all have the same mental model. Priya to send 1h trace + canonical prompts by Sep 4. Redwood sends harness + trace template by Sep 2. Daniel to draft measurement scripts. Then baseline run week of Sep 8. Deliverables: run CSVs, p95/p99 per window, cost estimate, and fallback playbook.
[09:34] Priya: Confirmed. Also please add a column for cache-hit reason in CSV.
[09:38] Daniel: Will do.
[09:40] Maya: Anything else?
[09:42] Liam: I'll confirm peering details and whether we can host the harness inside our GCP project.
[09:47] Rosa: I'll assemble the product acceptance criteria doc and share by Sep 4 as well.
[09:52] Maya: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up with a calendar invite for kickoff and attach the docs.
[09:58] Priya: Thanks all, bye.
[10:00] (call ends)

Notes: Transcript contains light ASR errors and speaker overlap at times; timestamps approximate.
file_notes: POC scoping focused on SLOs that combine TTFT and TPOT, measurement windows (5s/30s/5m), replay vs synthetic, and acceptance criteria. Distinct action owners and deadlines captured.
